question:
A mathematics class is evaluating a definite integral without using a limit of sums. The function under consideration is $f(x)=2x^3-3x^2+4$ on the closed interval $[1,3]$. Since $f$ is a polynomial, it is continuous throughout this interval. The students are instructed to find an antiderivative $F(x)$ and then use the values of the same antiderivative at the upper and lower limits. They also discuss why an arbitrary constant need not be retained when evaluating a definite integral. The investigation focuses on the second form of the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus and the connection between antiderivatives and definite integrals.

(a) Explain why the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus can be applied to $f(x)$ on $[1,3]$.

(b) Find an antiderivative $F(x)$ of $f(x)$.

(c) Evaluate $\int_1^3(2x^3-3x^2+4)\,dx$.

(d) Justify why adding an arbitrary constant to $F(x)$ does not change the value of the definite integral.
explanation:
(a)
The function $f(x)=2x^3-3x^2+4$ is a polynomial. Polynomial functions are continuous for all real $x$, so $f$ is continuous on the closed interval $[1,3]$. Therefore, the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus can be applied.

(b)
Integrating term by term, $$F(x)=\int(2x^3-3x^2+4)\,dx=\frac{x^4}{2}-x^3+4x$$ An arbitrary constant is unnecessary for evaluating the definite integral.

(c)
By the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus, $$\int_1^3(2x^3-3x^2+4)\,dx=F(3)-F(1)$$ Now, $$F(3)=\frac{81}{2}-27+12=\frac{51}{2}$$ and $$F(1)=\frac{1}{2}-1+4=\frac{7}{2}$$ Hence, $$\int_1^3(2x^3-3x^2+4)\,dx=\frac{51}{2}-\frac{7}{2}=22$$

(d)
If $F(x)+C$ is used instead of $F(x)$, then $$[F(3)+C]-[F(1)+C]=F(3)-F(1)$$ because the two occurrences of $C$ cancel. Thus, the arbitrary constant does not affect the value of a definite integral.

(c) The integral equals $44$
(d) The constant does not cancel
